ety.text: First attested in the 1530s. From French abusif, from Latin abūsīvus, from abusus + -ivus (“-ive”). Equivalent to abuse + -ive.

senses.d: Prone to treat someone badly by coarse, insulting words or other maltreatment; vituperative; reproachful; scurrilous.
ex: All they could ever do was to shout abusive inanities at me.
"Zero Tolerance. Aggressive and abusive behavior will not be tolerated. Our team are here to help, not hurt," the signs read.

senses.d: Tending to deceive; fraudulent.
ex: an abusive treaty

senses.d: Tending to misuse; practising or containing abuse.
ex: the abusive prerogatives of his see

senses.d: Being physically or emotionally injurious; characterized by repeated violence or other abuse.
Wrongly used; perverted; misapplied; unjust; illegal.
ex: I am […]necessitated to use the word Parliament improperly, according to the abusive acceptation thereof.

senses.d: Catachrestic.

es:abusivo.gl: abusive (practising, containing or being an abuse)

From Middle English abusen, then from either Old French abus (“improper use”), or from Latin abūsus (“misused, using up”), perfect active participle of abūtor (“make improper use of, consume, abuse”), from ab (“away”) + ūtor (“to use”). Equivalent to ab- + use.

From Middle English abusen, from Middle French abuser, from Latin abūsus (“misused, using up”), perfect active participle of abūtor (“to use up, misuse, consume”), from ab (“from, away from”) + ūtor (“to use”).

senses.d: Improper treatment or usage; application to a wrong or bad purpose; an unjust, corrupt or wrongful practice or custom.
ex: human rights abuses
All abuse, whether physical, verbal, psychological or sexual, is bad.

senses.d: Misuse; improper use; perversion.
ex: Liberty may be endangered by the abuses of liberty, as well as by the abuses of power.

senses.d: A delusion; an imposture; misrepresentation; deception.
ex: Or is it some abuse, and no such thing?

senses.d: Coarse, insulting speech; abusive language; language that unjustly or angrily vilifies.
ex: children hurling abuse at each other
The two parties, after exchanging a good deal of abuse, came to blows.

senses.d: Catachresis.
Physical maltreatment; injury; cruel treatment.
Violation; defilement; rape; forcing of undesired sexual activity by one person on another, often on a repeated basis.
To put to a wrong use; to misapply; to use improperly; to use for a wrong purpose or end; to pervert
ex: He abused his authority.
This principle (if we may so abuse the word) shot rapidly into popularity

senses.d: To injure; to maltreat; to hurt; to treat with cruelty, especially repeatedly.
ex: And I would have things to say to this God at the judgement, storming at him, as Job stormed with the eloquence of the abused heart.

senses.d: To attack with coarse language; to insult; to revile; malign; to speak in an offensive manner to or about someone; to disparage.
ex: The […] tellers of news abused the general.
But ever and always curse him and abuse him.

senses.d: To imbibe a drug for a purpose other than it was intended; to intentionally take more of a drug than was prescribed for recreational reasons; to take illegal drugs habitually.
To violate; defile; to rape; (reflexive) to masturbate.
Misrepresent; adulterate.
ex: Believe me, sir, he hath been abused, grossly abused to you.

senses.d: To deceive; to trick; to impose on; misuse the confidence of.
Disuse.

From Middle English abundaunce, habaundance, from Old French habundance, abondance, from Latin abundantia (“fullness, plenty”), from abundō (“to overflow”). Equivalent to abound + -ance. Displaced Old English geniht (“abundance, plenty”).

senses.d: A large quantity; many.
ex: Due to the abundance of art material, the class made a giant collage.
There is not a great abundance of time, so please don't dawdle.

senses.d: An overflowing fullness or ample sufficiency; profusion; copious supply; superfluity; plentifulness.
ex: It is lamentable to remember what abundance of noble blood hath been shed with small benefit to the Christian state.

senses.d: Wealth; affluence; plentiful amount of resources.
Frequency, amount, ratio of something within a given environment or sample.
A political ideology that is progressive but prioritises economic growth and infrastructure construction.
A bid to take nine or more tricks in solo whist.
enough, sufficiency.

ety.text: First attested about 1380. From Middle English abundaunt, habundaunt, aboundant, from Anglo-Norman abundant, from Old French abondant, from Latin abundāns, present participle of abundō (“to overflow, to abound”). Compare abound.

senses.d: Fully sufficient; found in copious supply; in great quantity; overflowing.
ex: Blackberries are abundant in this part of the country in October, so we always make lots of jam.
an abundant selection of carpets to choose from

senses.d: Richly supplied; wealthy; possessing in great quantity.
ex: Abundant in goodness and truth.

senses.d: Being an abundant number, i.e. less than the sum of all of its divisors except itself.
